newsitem.title: MONGOLIA: Mongolia prime minister pledges to woo investors.
newsitem.headline: Mongolia prime minister pledges to woo investors.

text.p: Mongolian Prime Minister M. Enkhsaikhan has pledged to tackle the landlocked country's infrastructure problems that he described as a major obstacle to attracting foreign investment.
Improving the country's telecommunications and roads was central to the government's bid to open up the economy to free market principles, he said in a recent interview with Reuters.
"The difficulties with weak infrastructure are a problem for international investors," Enkhsaikhan said, adding that Mongolia hoped to attract foreign investment to its telecommunications sector.
"Japanese and Korean companies especially are investing a lot," he said. "We must aim to have a high-tech data communications system by the year 2000."
An underdeveloped road network was another source of concern, he said.
"The problems relating to road haulage require huge investment," Enkhsaikhan said.
Work was already under way, in partnership with Japanese companies, to develop the railway network, Enkhsaikhan said.
But possibly the next big play for investors in the transport sector would be the sell-off of the state owned Mongolian Airlines (MIAT).
The government was already in talks with advisers on the sale, he said, adding that he preferred the privatisation to be carried out through an international flotation.
But he was circumspect about how large a stake could be sold as well as potential revenues.
"It's hard to guess at this stage how much could be raised," he said. Flotation preparations were under way, he said.
"The official start could be this fall (autumn)," he said, adding that overseas consultants could be involved.
Trained as an economist, Enkhsaikhan has been in power just 10 months but has moved swiftly to push forward economic reforms.
He aims to privatise 200 state-owned businesses in the next 18 months and move toward private land ownership in this vast country lodged between China and Russia.
Enkhsaikhan's reformist party upset the formerly communist rulers in last year's parliamentary elections.

However, last month's presidential elections saw the formerly communist candidate elected by a landslide, raising the question of whether this signalled a rejection of his policies and a possible slackening in his ambitious pace of reform.
The prime minister dismissed the view that the presidential election showed he was losing public support for his policies as unemployment and inflation have risen.
"Mongolia has been on the road of transition since 1990. There was a change of power in 1996 and it wasn't because people were tired of the pace of reforms.
"In fact they wanted the pace to accelerate," he said, referring to his election platform of free market reform.

Privatisation and encouraging foreign investment were priorities. The government showcased opportunities at its first investment conference last week, highlighting mining, oil and gas as key areas suitable for international investors.
"Minerals and oil will be our major exports in future," he said. Currently cashmere and copper are the biggest exports.
